solution:
An amine is classified by the number of hydrogen atoms of ammonia that have been replaced by alkyl/aryl groups, i.e. by how many carbon groups are bonded to NITROGEN — not by the nature of the carbon that carries the nitrogen.

(i) Nitrogen carries one aryl group and two hydrogens \((-\text{NH}_2)\): **primary (1\(^\circ\))**.
(ii) Nitrogen carries one aryl group and two methyl groups, and no hydrogen: **tertiary (3\(^\circ\))**.
(iii) \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHNH}_2\): nitrogen carries a single alkyl group and two hydrogens: **primary (1\(^\circ\))**. The carbon bearing the nitrogen is a secondary carbon, but that does not make the amine secondary.
(iv) \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\): nitrogen carries two ethyl groups and one hydrogen: **secondary (2\(^\circ\))**.

(i) primary; (ii) tertiary; (iii) primary; (iv) secondary.

\(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{11}\text{N}\) fits \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+3}\text{N}\), so it is a saturated, acyclic amine with no ring and no multiple bond. Eight isomers are possible.

(i) and (ii) Structures with their IUPAC names:

Primary (four butyl groups):
1. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\) — Butan-1-amine
2. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CH}_3\) — Butan-2-amine
3. \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{NH}_2\) — 2-Methylpropan-1-amine
4. \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CNH}_2\) — 2-Methylpropan-2-amine

Secondary (two alkyl groups on N, four carbons in all):
5. \(\text{CH}_3\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — N-Methylpropan-1-amine
6. \(\text{CH}_3\text{NHCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) — N-Methylpropan-2-amine
7. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5\) — N-Ethylethanamine

Tertiary (three alkyl groups on N):
8. \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NC}_2\text{H}_5\) — N,N-Dimethylethanamine

(iii) Types of isomerism shown by different pairs:
- **Chain isomerism** — where the carbon skeleton differs, e.g. butan-1-amine and 2-methylpropan-1-amine.
- **Position isomerism** — where the \(-\text{NH}_2\) group sits on a different carbon of the same chain, e.g. butan-1-amine and butan-2-amine.
- **Metamerism** — where the same class of amine carries different alkyl groups about the nitrogen, e.g. N-ethylethanamine and N-methylpropan-1-amine.
- **Functional group isomerism** — between a primary, a secondary and a tertiary amine, e.g. butan-1-amine, N-ethylethanamine and N,N-dimethylethanamine.

(i) Benzene into aniline — nitrate, then reduce the nitro group:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[323-333\ \text{K}]{\text{conc. HNO}_3 / \text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow[(\text{ii})\ \text{NaOH}]{(\text{i})\ \text{Sn}/\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)

(ii) Benzene into N,N-dimethylaniline — make aniline as above, then alkylate exhaustively at nitrogen with two moles of methyl halide:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{2\,\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + 2\,\text{HCl}\)
A base such as \(\text{NaHCO}_3\) is used to remove the HCl formed, so the amine is not tied up as its salt.

(iii) \(\text{Cl}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{Cl}\) into hexane-1,6-diamine — the target has SIX carbons and the dihalide only four, so one carbon must be added at each end. Use cyanide (ascent of the series) and reduce:
\(\text{Cl}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{2\,\text{KCN (alc.)}} \text{N} \equiv \text{C}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{C} \equiv \text{N} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}} \text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2\)
Hexanedinitrile is reduced (catalytically, or with \(\text{LiAlH}_4\)) to hexane-1,6-diamine.

Two effects decide the answers. An aryl group attached DIRECTLY to nitrogen delocalises the lone pair into the ring, so it is much less available for protonation — aromatic amines are therefore far weaker bases than ammonia. Alkyl groups release electrons (+I) and so raise basicity; in AQUEOUS solution the order is not simply 3\(^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ\), because the substituted ammonium ion is also stabilised by hydrogen bonding to water, and the more alkyl groups it carries the fewer N–H hydrogens are left for solvation and the greater the steric crowding.

(i) Aniline is weakest. Ammonia has no alkyl group at all. In benzylamine the ring is one carbon away from nitrogen, so there is no conjugation with the lone pair and it behaves as an aliphatic amine, though the phenyl group's \(-\text{I}\) effect makes it slightly weaker than ethylamine. Diethylamine, a secondary aliphatic amine, is the strongest in water.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 < \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\)

(ii) Aniline is again weakest. Among the ethyl amines in water the interplay of the inductive effect, solvation and steric hindrance gives \(2^\circ > 3^\circ > 1^\circ\).
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} < (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}\)

(iii) Aniline is weakest; benzylamine next, since the ring is insulated from nitrogen by the \(-\text{CH}_2-\) group but still exerts \(-\text{I}\). Among the methyl amines in water the order is \(2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ\), trimethylamine falling behind because its three methyl groups leave only one N–H for solvation and crowd the nitrogen.
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 < \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 < (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{N} < \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 < (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}\)

solution:
An amine is a Lewis base: the unshared pair on nitrogen accepts the proton of the acid, giving a substituted ammonium salt.

(i) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}\)
Product: propan-1-aminium chloride (propylammonium chloride).

(ii) \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}\)
Product: N,N-diethylethanaminium chloride (triethylammonium chloride).

Both salts are ionic, soluble in water and insoluble in ether, and both regenerate the free amine on treatment with a strong base such as NaOH.

Aniline is alkylated successively at nitrogen. With an EXCESS of methyl iodide the alkylation runs to the stage at which nitrogen carries no hydrogen left to replace:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{I}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{I}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{I}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}(\text{CH}_3)_3\ \overset{-}{\text{I}}\)
The final alkylation product is N,N,N-trimethylanilinium iodide. Alkylation stops here because the quaternary nitrogen has no N–H bond and no lone pair left.

Sodium carbonate solution has two effects. Each alkylation step liberates HI; the carbonate neutralises it, so the amine stays free instead of being converted to its unreactive hydroiodide salt and the reaction can proceed to the quaternary stage:
\(2\,\text{HI} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\,\text{NaI} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\)
Acting on the quaternary salt itself, the aqueous carbonate exchanges the iodide for hydroxide:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}(\text{CH}_3)_3\ \overset{-}{\text{I}} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{N}}(\text{CH}_3)_3\ \overset{-}{\text{O}}\text{H} + \text{NaI} + \text{NaHCO}_3\)
giving N,N,N-trimethylanilinium hydroxide.
_note: The stem is open to two readings — whether the sodium carbonate is a condition OF the alkylation or a reagent acting ON the final product. Both are answered above rather than one being chosen silently.

solution:
This is benzoylation, a nucleophilic substitution at the acyl carbon in which the hydrogen of \(-\text{NH}_2\) is replaced by the benzoyl group:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOC}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{HCl}\)
The reaction is carried out in the presence of a base (aqueous NaOH, the Schotten-Baumann conditions, or pyridine), which removes the HCl formed and drives the equilibrium to the right.

Product: N-Phenylbenzamide (benzanilide).

\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_9\text{N}\) fits \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+3}\text{N}\), so it is a saturated acyclic amine. Four isomers are possible:

Primary:
1. \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\) — Propan-1-amine
2. \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHNH}_2\) — Propan-2-amine

Secondary:
3. \(\text{CH}_3\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5\) — N-Methylethanamine

Tertiary:
4. \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{N}\) — N,N-Dimethylmethanamine

Only PRIMARY ALIPHATIC amines liberate nitrogen gas with nitrous acid. They give an aliphatic diazonium salt which, having no ring to delocalise the positive charge, is far too unstable to survive and at once loses \(\text{N}_2\) quantitatively, the alcohol being formed:
\(\text{R}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{HNO}_2 \rightarrow [\text{R}-\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}}] \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{R}-\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{HCl}\)
Secondary amines give an N-nitrosoamine and tertiary amines merely form a salt, so neither evolves nitrogen.

The isomers that liberate nitrogen gas are **propan-1-amine** and **propan-2-amine**.

(i) 3-Methylaniline into 3-nitrotoluene.
Direct nitration is useless here: in the strongly acidic nitrating mixture the amine is protonated to the meta-directing anilinium ion, and the amino group is also oxidised. Instead, convert the amino group into a diazonium group and replace it by \(-\text{NO}_2\), which fixes the substituent at exactly the carbon the amino group occupied:
\(3\text{-CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} 3\text{-CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{Cl}} \xrightarrow{\text{HBF}_4} 3\text{-CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\ \overset{-}{\text{B}}\text{F}_4 \xrightarrow[\text{Cu},\ \Delta]{\text{NaNO}_2} 3\text{-CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NO}_2\)
The last step gives 3-nitrotoluene, together with \(\text{N}_2\) and \(\text{NaBF}_4\).

(ii) Aniline into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.
The \(-\text{NH}_2\) group is a powerful activating, o-/p-directing group, so aniline with bromine water brominates at all three available ortho and para positions in one step. The amino group has then done its work and is removed through the diazonium salt:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \xrightarrow{3\,\text{Br}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}} 2,4,6\text{-tribromoaniline} \xrightarrow[273-278\ \text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{the diazonium chloride} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}} 1,3,5\text{-tribromobenzene}\)
Hypophosphorous acid (or ethanol) reduces the diazonium salt, replacing the \(-\overset{+}{\text{N}}_2\) group by hydrogen and releasing \(\text{N}_2\). Direct bromination of benzene could never give the 1,3,5-pattern, because bromine is itself o-/p-directing.
